explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says what you sow "…is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else." (1 Corinthians 15:37). Nobody plants a seed and expects to see that same little seed standing there in July. The seed is just where it starts.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He says what you sow "…is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else." (1 Corinthians 15:37). The seed is not the finished body. Picture a lump of dough that hasn't met the oven yet: nobody calls that a cookie, and I'd know.

That's it, baker. Paul says "…God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body." (1 Corinthians 15:38). The farmer drops the seed and walks off. The body is God's doing.

A farmer does the sowing, friend, but look at who Paul credits. He says "…God gives it a body as He has designed…" (1 Corinthians 15:38). The farmer drops the seed in the dirt and waits like the rest of us. Paul gives the giving of the body to God.

Rain is a nice guess, friend, and no seed is complaining about a good drink. But Paul names someone else: "…God gives it a body as He has designed…" (1 Corinthians 15:38). He gives each kind of seed its own body. The rain doesn't get the credit.
Right, baker. Paul says "Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). One list, four kinds. Nobody gets mixed up in this lineup.

Paul sees it differently, friend. He says "Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). That's four kinds, not one. A bird and a fish are not wearing the same thing.

explanations.answer: Men and animals share one kind
explanations.explanation: Close, but Paul keeps them apart, friend. He says "Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). Men get one kind and animals get another. Every group in his list has its own.

Look up again, friend. Paul says "The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor." (1 Corinthians 15:41). Sun, moon and stars each get their own. Even one star differs from the next.

That's right, baker. Paul says "The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor." (1 Corinthians 15:41). The sun, the moon and the stars each get their own degree. Even star differs from star, and I know a few skies where that's easy to see.

You got it, baker. Paul says "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). Perishable means it can wear out. Imperishable means it won't. My edges could use that kind of news.
Not quite, friend. Paul says "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). The body is not raised the same as it was sown. Something new has happened to it.

Nothing in the verse says anything about being unseen, friend. Paul says "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). Imperishable is the word he picks. It's about a body that doesn't wear out.

Yes, baker. Paul says "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). It's the same body, and the ending is nothing like the start. What is sown in dishonor is raised in glory, and he follows it with weakness turning into power.

I see why you'd go there, friend, since it sits near dishonor. But Paul says "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). He's not stacking one low word on another. He's flipping it.
Paul has a louder word than that, friend. He says "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). Glory is the opposite of dishonor. Silence never makes it into the verse.

That's the one, baker. Paul says "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). Then he adds, "If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body." He treats the second as just as real as the first.

Paul draws a line between the two, friend. He says "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). Sown is natural. Raised is spiritual. Same word wouldn't make a very good contrast.

Dust comes up later in the passage, friend, but not here. Paul says "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). The raised body is a spiritual one. Hold onto that dust thought for a minute.
Yes, baker. Paul says "The first man Adam became a living being…"; the last Adam "…a life-giving spirit." (1 Corinthians 15:45). The first one became a living being. The last one gives life.

That one belongs to the first Adam, friend. Paul says "The first man Adam became a living being…"; the last Adam "…a life-giving spirit." (1 Corinthians 15:45). Paul gives the last Adam a bigger title. He doesn't just have life, he gives it.

Earth does come up, friend, but it's a different Adam. Paul says "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). For the last Adam, verse 45 says "…a life-giving spirit." I'd mix those up too if I were rushing through the batch.

Right, baker. Paul says "The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual." (1 Corinthians 15:46). That's the order. Natural first, spiritual after, like mixing the dough before the oven.
Paul says it the other way around, friend. He says "The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual." (1 Corinthians 15:46). Natural comes first. The spiritual follows.
That's right, baker. Paul says "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). Dust for one, heaven for the other. Two very different starting points.

Eden is a fair guess, friend, since Adam was placed in the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:15). But Paul says "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). He names heaven for the second man. Eden isn't in this verse.

Egypt is a long way off from this passage, friend. Paul says "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). The second man is from heaven. No road trip needed.

Careful, friend. Paul says "…flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:50). He doesn't say it can, just as it is. Something has to change first.

Yes, baker. Paul says "…flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:50). The perishable can't inherit the imperishable. That's why the change in the next verses matters.
That's it, baker. Paul says "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). Some sleep and some don't, but nobody is left out of the change. All of us means all of us.

Not in this verse, friend. Paul says "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). The word is changed, not tested. Some will sleep and some won't, but all will be changed.

This mystery isn't a warning, friend. Paul says "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). The word is changed. He's telling them what's coming, and he calls it a mystery.

explanations.answer: In the twinkling of an eye
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says it happens "…in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). He adds that the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. That's how quick the change is.

explanations.answer: At the turning of a year
explanations.explanation: Way too slow, friend. Paul says "…in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). A year would be a very long wait. Paul says instant.

explanations.answer: In the passing of a day
explanations.explanation: Still too slow, friend. Paul says "…in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). A day is a whole lot of waiting. Paul says an instant, and he means it.

That's right, baker. Paul says "…the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality." (1 Corinthians 15:53). Paul talks about being clothed, like putting on something new. Mortal gets covered by immortality.

Honor is a fair guess, friend, since Paul talks about dishonor and glory earlier (1 Corinthians 15:43). But here he says "…the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality." (1 Corinthians 15:53). Mortal pairs with immortality. Honor isn't the word in this verse.

Paul does talk about weakness and power earlier, friend (1 Corinthians 15:43). But in this verse he says "…the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality." (1 Corinthians 15:53). Mortal is paired with immortality. Strength isn't the word here.

explanations.answer: It is swallowed up in victory
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The saying is "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Death is the one getting swallowed. Not the other way around.

explanations.answer: It is held back for a season
explanations.explanation: That's a gentler ending than the one Paul gives, friend. The saying is "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Death isn't held back for a while. It's swallowed up.

explanations.answer: It is cast out of the land
explanations.explanation: No land in this one, friend. The saying is "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Swallowed up is the picture Paul gives, and it's a total one.
That's right, baker. Paul says "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." (1 Corinthians 15:56). He names sin as the sting of death. Then he adds that the power of sin is the law.
Fear is a good guess, friend, since death can sure feel scary. But Paul says "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." (1 Corinthians 15:56). The text names sin, not fear.
Pain makes sense to guess, friend, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." (1 Corinthians 15:56). Sin is the sting, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: Their labor in the Lord is not in vain
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Paul says "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). Not in vain means it counts. So keep those ovens warm.

explanations.answer: Others will see their good work
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason, friend. He says "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). The reason he names is that their labor is not in vain. That means the work done in the Lord isn't wasted, and that's what he wants them to know.

explanations.answer: Their reward will come in this life
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say when anything comes, friend, and he doesn't give that reason. He says "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). Not in vain means the labor isn't wasted. That's the reason he gives for staying at it.
